accessibility-policy.whyItMatters: An accessibility statement tells users what the project is trying to support, what remains limited, and how to report barriers.
minimum: State an accessibility goal.
Describe known limitations honestly.
Provide an accessible reporting route.
stronger: List tested browsers, devices, and assistive technologies.
Publish automated and manual test status.
Explain prioritization, response expectations, and available workarounds.
commonMistakes: Claiming full WCAG conformance without evidence.
Listing only automated test results.
Making the reporting process itself inaccessible.
exampleEvidence: An accessibility issue form that avoids sensitive information.

resources.label: Open Source Guides: Accessibility Best Practices

accessibility-verification.whyItMatters: Automated checks catch repeatable problems, but human testing is needed to evaluate real keyboard, screen-reader, zoom, contrast, motion, and device use.
minimum: Run automated accessibility checks for relevant interface changes.
Test keyboard navigation and visible focus.
Record known manual-testing gaps.
stronger: Test desktop and mobile screen readers.
Verify zoom, reflow, forced colors, reduced motion, touch, and physical devices.
Publish findings and create follow-up issues.
commonMistakes: Treating a perfect automated score as proof of accessibility.
Testing only one browser or viewport.
Closing accessibility work without documenting failures.
exampleEvidence: Issues linked to screen-reader, reflow, or device findings.

resources.label: Open Source Guides: Accessibility Best Practices

conduct-enforcement.whyItMatters: A Code of Conduct is credible only when reports can be handled privately, consistently, and without conflicts of interest.
minimum: Define who receives reports and who may access them.
Describe proportionate enforcement options.
Protect reporters and participants from retaliation.
stronger: Provide conflict-safe handling for reports involving a maintainer.
Set acknowledgement, evidence, outcome, and reconsideration expectations.
Document confidentiality limits and platform escalation.
commonMistakes: Publishing rules without deciding who enforces them.
Sharing private report details more widely than necessary.
Treating an unproven report as knowingly false.
exampleEvidence: A conduct enforcement section with an escalation ladder.
A documented private reporting route and anti-retaliation statement.

resources.label: Open Source Guides: Code of Conduct

private-vulnerability-reporting.whyItMatters: Private vulnerability reporting reduces the chance that exploitable details are exposed before maintainers can assess and address them.
minimum: Provide a verified private route.
Explain what information helps triage.
Ask reporters not to publish exploit details prematurely.
stronger: Enable platform-native private vulnerability reporting.
Document acknowledgement and coordinated-disclosure expectations.
Separate security reports from ordinary support requests.
commonMistakes: Publishing a contact address that is not monitored.
Requesting passwords, tokens, or unnecessary personal information.
Guaranteeing rewards or response times the project cannot provide.
exampleEvidence: A monitored security email or private advisory form.
A tested path from report intake to incident response.

resources.label: Open Source Guides: Security Best Practices

threat-model.whyItMatters: A lightweight threat model helps maintainers identify important assets, trust boundaries, misuse cases, and residual risks before incidents occur.
minimum: List important assets and trust boundaries.
Identify realistic misuse cases.
Record current mitigations and remaining risk.
stronger: Assign owners and review triggers.
Cover repository, dependency, workflow, release, and deployment risks.
Revisit the model after architecture or permission changes.
commonMistakes: Writing a generic list unrelated to the actual architecture.
Treating the model as proof that risk is eliminated.
Ignoring non-server risks such as imports, browser storage, or CI permissions.
exampleEvidence: THREAT_MODEL.md with assets, threats, mitigations, and residual risk.
A diagram or table of trust boundaries.

resources.label: Open Source Guides: Security Best Practices

incident-response.whyItMatters: An incident-response plan reduces confusion when maintainers need to assess, contain, fix, verify, and communicate a security problem.
minimum: Define report intake and triage.
Identify containment, remediation, and verification steps.
Explain how users will be informed when necessary.
stronger: Assign decision authority and backups.
Keep a private incident log and public disclosure criteria.
Record lessons learned and update tests or the threat model.
commonMistakes: Improvising roles during an active incident.
Publishing uncertain details too early.
Closing an incident without follow-up actions.
exampleEvidence: A post-incident review linked to remediation issues.

resources.label: Open Source Guides: Security Best Practices

contributor-onboarding.whyItMatters: Clear contributor pathways help people move from reporting a small issue to making repeat contributions and taking trusted responsibility.
minimum: Explain first-contribution steps.
Offer small, well-scoped tasks.
Describe review and communication expectations.
stronger: Recognize documentation, testing, accessibility, design, triage, and community work.
Use contributor labels and release recognition.
Explain how regular contributors may gain permissions.
commonMistakes: Equating contribution only with code.
Leaving beginner issues too broad.
Promoting contributors without discussing responsibilities and security.
exampleEvidence: Release notes recognizing different contribution types.

support-boundaries.whyItMatters: Support boundaries protect users from unclear expectations and help maintainers avoid unsustainable commitments.
minimum: List supported request types and channels.
State that work is best effort and issues are not promises.
Explain out-of-scope requests.
stronger: Set realistic acknowledgement targets.
Distinguish normal support from security, accessibility, and conduct reports.
Document pauses, stale triage, and maintainer availability.
commonMistakes: Promising immediate help from a volunteer project.
Mixing confidential reports with public support.
Leaving users uncertain whether a request is accepted, deferred, or declined.
exampleEvidence: Issue triage outcomes and response targets.

succession.whyItMatters: Continuity planning protects users, releases, and community spaces when a maintainer pauses, becomes unavailable, or steps down.
minimum: Document temporary absence and archival options.
Identify which services and permissions must remain recoverable.
Explain how stewardship may transfer.
stronger: Maintain least-privilege backup access.
Define successor selection and consent.
Review continuity after service, account, or maintainer changes.
commonMistakes: Sharing credentials instead of granting named access.
Assuming a successor without their agreement.
Leaving release and deployment ownership undocumented.
exampleEvidence: Governance sections for absence, succession, and transfer.
A tested recovery route for repository and deployment access.

resources.label: Open Source Guides: Leadership and Governance

project-metrics.whyItMatters: A small set of goal-linked metrics can reveal project load, responsiveness, participation, and release progress without turning popularity into a health score.
minimum: Choose a few metrics connected to project goals.
Record how often they are reviewed.
Avoid collecting private user assessment data.
stronger: Track first-time and returning contributors, response times, backlog, releases, accessibility work, and roadmap outcomes.
Explain limitations and context.
Use aggregate repository data instead of invasive website tracking.
commonMistakes: Treating stars or page views as proof of health.
Measuring activity without a decision it supports.
Pressuring maintainers to maximize output.
exampleEvidence: METRICS.md with definitions and review cadence.
Documented privacy limits and interpretation notes.

dependency-asset-licensing.whyItMatters: A project may use code, actions, documentation, images, fonts, or other assets whose licenses and attribution requirements differ from the project license.
minimum: Inventory third-party dependencies and assets.
Check license compatibility and attribution requirements.
Remove or replace material with unclear permission.
stronger: Automate dependency-license checks where appropriate.
Maintain third-party notices.
Review licensing during pull requests and releases.
commonMistakes: Assuming the project license covers third-party material.
Copying screenshots, logos, or snippets without permission.
Adding a contributor agreement without a real need.
exampleEvidence: Pull-request checks for new third-party material.

protected-repository-access.whyItMatters: Least-privilege access and protected release paths reduce accidental or malicious changes to source code, workflows, tags, and deployments.
minimum: Use multi-factor authentication for privileged accounts.
Limit write access to people who need it.
Review default-branch and release settings.
stronger: Require appropriate checks or review for important changes.
Pin or review trusted automation actions.
Document permission grants, reviews, and removal.
commonMistakes: Sharing account credentials.
Granting administrator access for routine contributions.
Assuming a public repository does not need access controls.
exampleEvidence: Regular review of repository, CI, and deployment access.
